props.title: Thunderheart

sections.content: Thunderheart stands as one of Hollywood's more nuanced portrayals of Native American issues, drawing inspiration from the real-life events at Wounded Knee in 1973. Director Michael Apted, who previously documented Native American activism in his documentary Incident at Oglala (1992), brings authenticity by casting actual Lakota people and filming on location in the Badlands. The film follows the template of Dances with Wolves (1990) but takes a grittier, more contemporary approach, addressing uranium mining, tribal politics, and FBI interference on reservations.

sections.content: The film's strength lies in Val Kilmer's portrayal of Ray Levoi, an FBI agent discovering his Native heritage while investigating a murder. Unlike similar "white savior" narratives, Thunderheart subverts expectations by having Levoi learn from, rather than lead, the tribal community. Graham Greene's performance as tribal police officer Walter Crow Horse provides the film's moral center, while John Trudell, a real-life Native American activist, brings gravitas to his role as Jimmy Looks Twice.

The cinematography by Roger Deakins captures the stark beauty of South Dakota's Badlands, making the landscape a character itself. The film's supernatural elements, including Levoi's visions and spiritual experiences, are handled with respect rather than exploitation. This approach was revolutionary for 1992, predating later thoughtful Indigenous representations in films like Smoke Signals (1998) and The New World (2005). sections.content: Thunderheart marked a significant shift from Hollywood's traditional portrayal of Native Americans. While Dances with Wolves (1990) broke ground with its sympathetic portrayal, Thunderheart tackled contemporary issues facing Native communities. This paved the way for films like Skins (2002) and Wind River (2017), which continue to explore modern reservation life and systemic injustices.
